title: He wept over it (Luke 19:41–44)
hookLine: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem: if thou hadst known the things for peace

lines: A CHURCH SHAPED LIKE A TEAR.
cards: On the western slope of the Mount of Olives there's a small church shaped like a teardrop. It was built in the 1950s, and its name is Latin: Dominus Flevit, the Lord wept.

Behind the altar, a big window looks straight across the valley at the old city of Jerusalem, so the priest at Mass faces the view. On the front of the altar is a mosaic of a hen gathering her chicks.
The church marks one moment. Jesus has come down the hill on a colt, with crowds shouting praise. And then, at the sight of the city, he stops.

teach.b: It's what Christians call Palm Sunday. Crowds are spreading their cloaks on the road, shouting blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord.

teach.h: WEPT ALOUD, NOT A QUIET TEAR.
teach.b: In the middle of that joyful procession, Luke says: "And when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it." Luke's word means to weep aloud, to sob.
Then he speaks to the city: "If thou also hadst known, and that in this thy day, the things that are to thy peace; but now they are hidden from thy eyes." There's a play on words in it.
Many people heard the name Jerusalem as containing shalom, peace.

teach.h: THE CITY OF PEACE MISSED PEACE.
teach.b: The city of peace hasn't recognized what makes for peace. Then he grieves over what's coming: enemies will surround the city, and not leave a stone upon a stone, because thou hast not known the time of thy visitation.

Christians later read these words in light of what happened about forty years after: in the year 70 the Roman army besieged Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple, and many thousands died. Hear it the way Jesus says it.
He doesn't gloat. He doesn't curse. He weeps, the way you'd weep over a child running toward a road.

teach.h: THE THINGS THAT ARE TO THY PEACE.
teach.b: Remember the hen: how often would I have gathered thy children. It's the same love. Catholics hear in this a God who isn't distant from the suffering of cities.
Before the stones fall, someone stood on a hill and cried for them by name.

how: Pilgrims in the Holy Land celebrate Mass at the Dominus Flevit chapel on the Mount of Olives, facing the old city, and Catholics pray for peace in Jerusalem and in places at war in the prayers of the faithful.

o: the moment God came close, and wasn't known
a festival held each year at the Temple
the city's welcome for a Roman governor

games.q: he wept over it — tap the pairs.
p: the things that are to thy peace

s: Jesus wept over Jerusalem in the middle of a joyful procession
Luke places it during the entry, as the crowds shouted praise.
Luke's word for wept means a single quiet tear
it means to weep aloud, to sob.
Jesus cursed Jerusalem when he saw it
he wept over it and grieved for what was coming.

games.q: you're riding into a city to cheers and palm branches. you look up and see it spread out below you. what happens?
o: you speed up to reach the Temple.
games.why: Luke says he wept over it: if thou hadst known the things that are to thy peace.

practice: Bring to mind one city where people are living through war or violence, and picture it from a hill, the way Jesus saw Jerusalem: rooftops, a market, a hospital, children going somewhere.

Let yourself feel something for the people there, without needing to fix it or take a side. If you pray, ask for the things that make for peace there; if you don't, hold them in your attention with care.

wordCard.voice: Visitation. The time Jerusalem didn't know, when Jesus looked at the city in the middle of a joyful procession and sobbed. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he wept aloud, sobbed. A stronger word than the quiet tears at Lazarus' tomb in John.

carryVoice: Your line: the things for peace. Grief, not gloating, from the hill. Day four hundred seventy-seven, done.
